questions.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
2{x}^{2}+7x+6.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($2\times 6=12$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($7$).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of $12.$

The positive factor pairs of $12$ are

$$
(1,12),\,(2,6),\,(3,4).
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(3,4)$ add to $7:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}3+4 & =7\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $3x+4x,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+7x+6 & = \\ 2{x}^{2}+3x+4x+6 & = \\ (2{x}^{2}+3x)+(4x+6) & = \\ x(2x+3)+2(2x+3) & = \\ (x+2)(2x+3) & \end{aligned}
$$

Remember that the square root of a perfect square can be simplified using absolute value.

$$
\sqrt{{x}^{2}}=|x|
$$

Also, we notice that $64$ and ${p}^{2}$ are both perfect squares.

First, we write the expression under the square root as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{64{p}^{2}} & =\sqrt{{8}^{2}\cdot {p}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8\cdot 8\cdot p\cdot p} \\  & =\sqrt{8\cdot p\cdot 8\cdot p} \\  & =\sqrt{8p\cdot 8p} \\  & =\sqrt{(8p)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we take the absolute value of the squared quantity and simplify using the rules of absolute value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{(8p)^{2}} & =|8p| \\  & =|8|\cdot |p| \\  & =8|p|\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following values of $w$ satisfy the inequality $\frac{w}{4}<5\,?$

I. $w=24$

II. $w=20$

III. $w=8$
questions.worked_solution:
We substitute each value into the given inequality and check to see if the resulting statement is true or false.

- We substitute the value $w=24$ into the given inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{w}{4} & <5 \\ \frac{24}{4} & <5 \\ 6 & <5\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $w=24$ into the inequality leads to a **false** statement. 

Therefore, $w=24$ **does not satisfy** this inequality.

- We substitute the value $w=20$ into the given inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{w}{4} & <5 \\ \frac{20}{4} & <5 \\ 5 & <5\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $w=20$ into the inequality leads to a **false** statement. 

Therefore, $w=20$ **does not satisfy** this inequality.

- We substitute the value $w=8$ into the given inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{w}{4} & <5 \\ \frac{8}{4} & <5 \\ 2 & <5\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $w=8$ into the inequality leads to a **true** statement. 

Therefore, $w=8$ **satisfies** this inequality.

questions.problem: $40$ students took an algebra exam. If $12$ of them failed this exam, what percentage of students failed it?
questions.worked_solution:
We're given a part and a whole, and we must find a percentage. So, we can use the following formula:

$$
\text{percentage}=\text{part}÷\text{whole}
$$

In this case, 

- the part is the number of students that failed the exam, which is $12,$ and

- the whole is the total number of students, which is $40.$

Substituting our numbers into the above formula, we get

$$
\text{percentage}=12÷40=\frac{12}{40}.
$$

We can simplify this fraction as follows:

$$
\frac{12}{40}=\frac{12÷4}{40÷4}=\frac{3}{10}
$$

To write this as a percentage, we create an equivalent fraction with $100$ as the denominator:

$$
\frac{3}{10}=\frac{3\times 10}{10\times 10}=\frac{30}{100}
$$

Now we can write this fraction as a percentage:

$$
\frac{30}{100}=30%
$$

Therefore, $30%$ of the students failed the exam.

First, let's swap the left and right-hand sides so that the variable is on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a}{9} & =-3 \\ 9\cdot \frac{a}{9} & =9\cdot (-3) \\ \frac{9a}{9} & =-27 \\ \frac{\cancel{9}a}{\cancel{9}} & =-27 \\ a & =-27\end{aligned}
$$
